By noon the water had risen far enough to cover the mudflats where the previous week's traps had been set. Two of the traps were recovered intact; the rest will be collected tomorrow if the weather holds.
The team logged salinity readings at six stations and photographed erosion at the northern bank, which has widened noticeably since spring. Farther out, the channel markers had shifted during the winter storms, and a pair of dolphins surfaced twice near the boat without approaching. In the afternoon a small boat delivered fuel and replacement batteries, along with news that the bridge road would stay closed for another month. Everyone agreed the detour was tolerable, though it adds nearly an hour to the drive back to the station. Before dinner the crew compared notes and marked the day's positions on the chart.
Morning fog delayed the first launch, so the crew spent an hour checking the outboard motor and sorting the sample bottles by size. The fog lifted around ten, revealing a line of clouds stacked along the horizon and a pair of herons standing motionless at the edge of the reeds. Sampling went quickly after that. Each bottle was labeled with the station number and the time, then packed in ice for the drive back. The last transect crossed a shallow channel where the current ran harder than the chart suggested, and the boat had to be poled through by hand.
By late afternoon the wind had dropped and the water lay almost flat, reflecting the gulls that circled above the sandbar. The crew finished the remaining measurements early and began drying the samples in the shed behind the boathouse. There was talk of finishing the survey a day ahead of schedule if the weather held through the weekend.
